rationale:
bugs_open/258 defects 1 and 2, in the Thunder provision path. Owner-directed sequence (2026-08-13): fix these BEFORE unpausing, so the first unpaused provision can actually succeed instead of burning money on a run we already know fails.

DEFECT 1 — the adapter sent a constant cpu_cores: 4 whenever the caller supplied no vcpus, and Thunder rejects that for 9 of its 11 single-GPU specs. Re-measured live 2026-08-13 from GET /v1/specs, independently of the original filing, and it matches exactly: a6000 accepts [6,8]; a100xl [8,12,16]; l40 [6,8,12]; the *_production specs want exactly one value (15, or 10 for l40); only h100_x1/h100_x1_prototyping accept 4. Since h100 is the DEAREST GPU on the menu ($2.19/hr), 'provision with defaults' meant 'provision the most expensive box, or get a 400'. That asymmetry is also why the bug survived: anyone who tested with the expensive box saw it work.

A constant cannot be right here — no single value is valid across the specs — so the fix DERIVES the count from the catalogue rather than tabulating it in our source, where it would drift the moment Thunder changes. Only consulted when the caller said nothing, so an explicit request is never blocked by a /specs outage; and when it cannot be resolved it REFUSES rather than falling back, because falling back to a constant is precisely the bug.

DEFECT 2 — waitTimeout was a hardcoded 5 minutes with no config path. No measured a6000 boot met it (4m39s and 4m49s in, still STARTING), so WaitForRunning hit its deadline and the compensating cleanup DELETED the instance we had just started paying for. The compensation itself was correct and fired cleanly; the deadline it compensated for was wrong. Boot time is a vendor property, not ours to guess, so this becomes live config (migration 397) rather than a bigger constant needing a build and a fleet release every time Thunder drifts.

THE COUPLING REVIEWERS SHOULD PRESS ON, because it bites in the counter-intuitive direction: the adapter's wait MUST stay BELOW the dispatching step's timeout_seconds (600s on gpu-provisioner's dispatch_provision). If it exceeds it, a slow-but-SUCCESSFUL provision becomes the bad case — the await expires, the chassis retry driver re-dispatches, the bugs_open/259 claim guard refuses the duplicate (correctly, no second box), and the workflow reports FAILED while a real, running, billed instance sits there with nobody watching it. Hence the 397 default of 540s: well above the 5 minutes that demonstrably was not enough, well below the 600s await, with ~60s headroom for the create/keypair/secret/INSERT either side. Raising it further requires raising the STEP timeout FIRST, in that order.

WHY THIS IS ONLY SAFE NOW. Raising the wait makes the handler block longer, and a longer block used to mean MORE duplicate billing — the 258/259 interaction that made this unsafe to fix first. 259's claim guard is live as of thunder-adapter v1.0.1295 (build stamp 69612d692, verified by ancestry against the running pod), so a re-dispatch can no longer build a second box. Do not revert migration 396 and leave this raised.

Defect 3 of 258 (a failed provision leaving no durable record) is ALREADY FIXED by 259's claims table — status='failed' plus last_error plus the vendor id now survive pod-log rotation — so it is not in this plan.

plan.summary: Derive the default vCPU count from Thunder's own /v1/specs catalogue instead of a constant that is invalid for 9 of 11 single-GPU specs, and move the wait-for-RUNNING deadline into thunder_config so a slow-booting box is no longer destroyed at 5 minutes.

edits.rationale: Types plus the two pure helpers the derivation needs. SpecsResponse exists because the '{"specs": {...}}' wrapper is real: decoding /v1/specs straight into a map[string]Spec compiles, succeeds, and returns an EMPTY map — which would read as 'Thunder sells nothing' rather than as a decode bug. LowestValidVCPUs returns 0 rather than a fallback when a spec publishes no options, so the caller must decide, and the caller refuses.

GET /specs through the existing do() helper, matching ListInstances' shape. Read-only and free. Treats an empty catalogue as an error rather than an empty map, for the same reason as above — a silent empty result here would propagate as a guessed vCPU count.

Replaces `req.VCPUs = api.DefaultCPUCores` with a catalogue lookup, and REORDERS the default-resolution block so gpu/mode normalisation happens BEFORE the vCPU derivation — the spec key is built from gpu+count+mode, so deriving first would look up the wrong key (or an empty one). The lookup tries '<gpu>_x<n>_<mode>' then falls back to the bare '<gpu>_x<n>' key, which exists, carries no mode field and matches the prototyping options (verified live). Refuses on an unresolvable spec, naming the key so an operator can check it against /v1/specs.
Adds GetSpecs to the injectable interface so the derivation is testable without httptest, consistent with how CreateInstance/WaitForRunning/DeleteInstance are already injected.

The deadline as live config, default 540s, CHECK bounded 60..1800. The column comment and the file header both state the coupling to the dispatching step's timeout_seconds and the order to change them in, because raising this alone silently converts a slow SUCCESS into a reported FAILURE with a live billed box behind it. The verify block INDUCES a check violation rather than trusting the catalogue, and also asserts the default has not been set above the 600s await.
edits.sketch:
ALTER TABLE thunder_config ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS provision_wait_timeout_seconds integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 540
  CONSTRAINT thunder_config_provision_wait_bounds CHECK (provision_wait_timeout_seconds BETWEEN 60 AND 1800);

edits.rationale: Reads the new column through `(to_jsonb(t)->>'provision_wait_timeout_seconds')::int` DELIBERATELY, not as a bare column reference. A bare reference makes LoadConfig — and therefore every provision, decommission and reaper run — fail outright on any deployment where 397 has not been applied, coupling the binary to the migration in the direction that breaks production. to_jsonb of a missing key is simply NULL, so an unmigrated database degrades to the compiled-in default. Same row, same round trip, nullable field.
edits.sketch:
SELECT ..., (to_jsonb(t)->>'provision_wait_timeout_seconds')::int FROM thunder_config t LIMIT 1
// Config.ProvisionWaitTimeoutSeconds sql.NullInt64 — NULL means 'use the compiled-in default'

edits.rationale: Uses the configured deadline, falling back to the compiled-in default when absent, zero or out of range, and LOGGING whenever it falls back — a silently-defaulted deadline is indistinguishable from a configured one, which is exactly how a hardcoded 5 minutes went unnoticed until it deleted a box we had paid for. The 30-minute ceiling in code mirrors the migration's CHECK so a hand-edited row, or a future migration that drops the constraint, still cannot hand the adapter an absurd deadline.

Asserts on cpu_cores AS SENT TO THUNDER across the whole real catalogue, not on our defaulting logic agreeing with itself — the 400 came from the wire. The fixture is the live 2026-08-13 /v1/specs data, because 258 defect 1 is precisely a case where a plausible-looking invented constant was wrong. PROVEN ABLE TO FAIL: restoring the constant fails 7 of 8 cases, and the single survivor is h100_x1_prototyping — the one spec that accepts 4, which reproduces the exact asymmetry that hid the bug. Also covers: an explicit vcpus bypasses the catalogue (specs outage must not block it), an unresolvable spec refuses WITHOUT reaching the vendor, the wait deadline comes from config with safe fallbacks, and a guard that the 397 default stays below the dispatch await.

grounded_in: GET /v1/specs, re-measured live 2026-08-13 (single-GPU entries only): a100xl_x1 [8,12,16]; a100xl_x1_production [15]; a100xl_x1_prototyping [8,12,16]; a6000_x1 [6,8]; a6000_x1_prototyping [6,8]; h100_x1 [4,8,12,16]; h100_x1_production [15]; h100_x1_prototyping [4,8,12,16]; l40_x1 [6,8,12]; l40_x1_production [10]; l40_x1_prototyping [6,8,12]. 9 of 11 reject 4. Matches bugs_open/258's original table exactly.
Live specs envelope shape: {"specs": {"<key>": {...}}} — an object under a wrapper, keyed by composite '<gpu>_x<count>[_<mode>]'; 32 keys total. The bare '<gpu>_x<n>' key carries no mode field.

bugs_open/258 defect 2's measured timeline: 13:52:13 create accepted (billing starts) -> 13:56:52 vendor still STARTING at 4m39s -> 13:57:13 'Compensating cleanup starting' reason='WaitForRunning failed' -> 13:57:14 POST /instances/0/delete 200. Paid ~5 minutes for nothing.
provision_action.go NewProvisionAction had `waitTimeout: 5 * time.Minute` with no config path; thunder_config's schema (read live) had no timeout column and there is no env var.
gpu-provisioner dispatch_provision config timeout_seconds = 600 (live agent_definitions, 2026-08-13) — the ceiling the adapter's wait must stay under.

thunder-adapter running v1.0.1295, build stamp 69612d692a4a07d61eea3f648e1152e0fd36fd0a; `git merge-base --is-ancestor 10659b419 69612d692` succeeds, so 259's claim guard IS live and a re-dispatch can no longer build a second box.

Mutation evidence: restoring `req.VCPUs = api.DefaultCPUCores` fails TestDefaultVCPUsAreValidForEveryGPU for a6000, a100xl x2 modes, l40 x2 modes, h100_production and the a100 alias — 7 of 8 — with h100_x1_prototyping the only pass.

258 defect 3 (no durable record of a failed provision) is already closed by migration 396's thunder_provision_claims: status='failed' + last_error + thunder_instance_id persist beyond pod-log rotation.
plan.risks: 1) A NEW VENDOR CALL ON THE PROVISION PATH. GetSpecs runs before each defaulted provision (not when vcpus is explicit). It is read-only and free, but it is another dependency between 'provision requested' and 'instance created', and if /specs is down a defaulted provision now REFUSES where it previously sent an invalid 4 and got a 400 — a different failure, arguably a clearer one, but a behaviour change. Explicit-vcpus callers are unaffected by design and there is a test pinning that. 2) LOWEST-VALID IS A COST CHOICE, NOT A PERFORMANCE ONE: vCPUs are billed above the included allowance, so the cheapest valid option is what a caller expressing no preference should get — but a training job that wanted more CPU must now say so. Previously it got 4 (or a 400), so nothing silently loses CPU it used to have. 3) THE WAIT/AWAIT COUPLING is the real hazard and it is documented in three places (migration header, column COMMENT, a test) rather than enforced in code — the adapter cannot see the step's timeout_seconds, so this is a stated invariant, not a mechanical one. A future session raising the column past 600 without raising the step will convert slow successes into reported failures with live billed boxes behind them. If reviewers want that mechanised, the honest options are a startup check that reads the gpu-provisioner row, or moving the await timeout into thunder_config too. 4) MIGRATION ORDERING is NOT critical this time, unlike 396: the to_jsonb read means an unmigrated database degrades to the compiled default rather than failing. 5) Neither defect is fixed until the next thunder-adapter build and a whole-fleet release, which the OWNER runs; provisioning stays PAUSED until then, and the first unpaused run is still the real test of both.
